2.0.1 AO1. Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth (Leeann Lewis-Waddell)

AO1 Model Comparison Table
Approach / Model What It Explains Evidence for / Against Data / Assumptions Fit with AO
Email Response Process (Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala 2016; Kumar 2021) How readers move from viewing a newsletter to clicking and eventually purchasing. Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala (2016) tested newsletter formats against a control, and Kumar (2021) found clicks had the strongest link to purchases. Both studies were conducted in commercial settings rather than a university newsletter. Requires page views, clicks, and reservation data. Assumes each stage can be measured separately. Strongest overall fit because it matches the stages Canva and OpenTable can measure.
Visual Attention and Heuristics (Kumar and Salo 2018; Skourou and Spiliotopoulos 2024) Where readers look in a newsletter and which elements they are most likely to click. Kumar and Salo (2018) found upper-left links earn higher click-through rates, and Skourou and Spiliotopoulos (2024) found large images capture attention. Images may also pull attention away from the button. Requires versions that differ in button placement or media while all other elements stay the same. Good fit for choosing the test variables, but does not connect clicks to reservations.
Cognitive Load and Information Overload (Bashirzadeh, Mai, and Faure 2022; Kong, Zhu, and Konstan 2021) Why adding too much content, or sending too many emails, can reduce engagement. Bashirzadeh, Mai, and Faure (2022) found combining visual elements increased unsubscribes, and Kong, Zhu, and Konstan (2021) found university recipients often ignore bulk email. Requires page views alongside clicks to separate a design problem from a readership problem. Useful boundary condition, but explains limits rather than what drives clicks.
Industry Best Practices (Go 2024; Jones 2023) Practical recommendations for email design and benchmark click-through rates. Both guides recommend strong visuals, bold CTAs near the top, and testing one variable at a time. Both are written by companies that sell marketing or reservation services. Assumes general benchmarks apply to RKR’s audience. Helpful for benchmarks, but too weak to serve as the main framework.

The Email Response Process is the strongest fit for AO1 because it follows readers from viewing the newsletter to clicking the “Reserve a Table” button to making a reservation. This sequence matches the data available through Canva and OpenTable, which allows each stage to be measured. Visual attention research supports the decision to test button placement and media, while cognitive load research explains why only one change will be tested at a time. As such, the combination of these frameworks fits AO1 better than relying on industry best practices alone.

The evidence shows that button placement and visual design both affect click-through rate, and that clicks are closely connected to purchases. What remains uncertain is whether these findings will hold for a university audience that may already be overwhelmed by bulk email. It is also unclear whether the mailing list can be segmented and whether OpenTable can attribute reservations to separate links. Since two of my teammates are analyzing Facebook and Instagram, this analysis will focus only on the newsletter and should not assume it is the only channel influencing reservations. AO1 was already revised to test button placement in Fall and media in Spring, so no further revision is needed at this stage.

2.0.2 AO2. Customer Experience Factors Associated With Overall Satisfaction (Carmen Jimenez)

AO2 Model Comparison Table
Approach / Model What It Explains Evidence for / Against Data / Assumptions Fit with AO
Multidimensional Restaurant Quality Framework (Ryu, Lee, and Kim 2012) Explains how food quality, service quality, and the physical environment relate to customer satisfaction and behavioral intentions. Ryu, Lee, and Kim (2012) support evaluating several restaurant-quality dimensions together. The original restaurant context differs from RKR. Requires guest ratings of food quality, service quality, physical environment, and satisfaction. Assumes guests can evaluate these dimensions separately. Strongest overall fit because it directly includes the three main experience dimensions measured in AO2.
Food Quality–Satisfaction Approach (Namkung and Jang 2007) Explains how food quality relates to customer satisfaction and behavioral intentions. Namkung and Jang (2007) support food quality as an important part of restaurant satisfaction. The approach focuses mainly on food rather than the entire dining experience. Requires guest ratings of food-related characteristics such as quality, presentation, enjoyment, and consistency. Good fit for the food-quality component of AO2, but too narrow to address the full objective alone.
Physical Environment / Atmospherics Approach (Han and Ryu 2009; Heung and Gu 2012) Explains how atmosphere and the physical environment relate to satisfaction and behavioral responses. Han and Ryu (2009) and Heung and Gu (2012) support the importance of the restaurant environment. This approach does not fully account for food or service quality. Requires guest evaluations of atmosphere and physical-environment characteristics such as cleanliness, comfort, décor, layout, and overall ambiance. Good fit for the atmosphere and physical-environment component, but not sufficient by itself to address AO2.
Customer Satisfaction–Behavioral Intentions Approach (Arora and Singer 2006) Explains how customer satisfaction relates to future intentions such as returning to or recommending a restaurant. Research supports a relationship between satisfaction and behavioral intentions, but stated intentions do not confirm actual future behavior. Requires measures of overall satisfaction, intention to return, and willingness to recommend. Useful secondary fit because AO2 includes return intention and recommendation, but it does not directly identify the strongest and weakest experience areas.

The Multidimensional Restaurant Quality Framework is the strongest fit for AO2 because it directly includes the three main experience dimensions measured in this objective: food quality, service quality, and the physical environment. Ryu, Lee, and Kim (2012) show that these dimensions are connected to customer satisfaction and behavioral intentions. This framework is broader than the food-quality and physical-environment approaches because it allows the dining experience to be evaluated as a combination of multiple factors rather than focusing on only one area.

The existing research shows that food quality, service quality, and atmosphere or physical environment are important parts of the restaurant experience. However, the literature cannot determine which of these areas RKR guests rate most positively or negatively. This is especially important because RKR is a student-operated restaurant located on a university campus, which may create a different guest experience from the restaurants studied in previous research. For this reason, AO2 still requires primary survey data from RKR guests. The current AO does not need to be revised because it is measurable, directly connected to the available survey data, and aligned with the project objective of identifying strengths and improvement opportunities in the RKR dining experience.

AO5 Model Comparison Table

Post-format comparison with support from S–O–R and Uses and Gratifications is the best fit for AO5. Comparing formats will help us see whether Reels, carousels, or single-image posts get stronger engagement for RKR. S–O–R helps explain how content might affect audience responses. Uses and Gratifications adds another explanation by looking at what people get from the content, such as information, entertainment, or social connection. Processing fluency helps explain why some food images may perform better. These theories do not tell us which format is best for RKR, so we still need to look at the account’s actual results. Past posts will be grouped by format to create a baseline, and new posts will be compared with those results. Engagement rate will be calculated using likes, comments, shares, and saves divided by reach, multiplied by 100.

The research suggests that both visual presentation and content purpose can affect engagement. Kulikovskaja et al. (2023) found different engagement patterns for informational and entertaining, reward-based, and relationship-focused restaurant content. However, the research does not establish what works best for RKR’s Instagram audience. We will need Instagram Insights data and information about each post’s topic, purpose, posting date, and whether it was promoted. For example, a Reel might perform better because it is entertaining, rather than just because it is a video. New posts should be measured over the same amount of time so the comparison is more useful. Stronger engagement also does not automatically mean more reservations. At this point, AO5 does not need a major revision, although adding “among the formats tested” would make it more specific. We still need faculty guidance on how far back to look at past posts and how many new posts to test.

2.1 Investigation of Currently Available Research Framework/Model

2.1.1 AO1. Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth (Leeann Lewis-Waddell)

Analytics Objective: Compare “Reserve a Table” click rates and attributed OpenTable reservations across RKR newsletter section designs, testing button placement in Fall 2026 and image versus video in Spring 2027.

Existence of Well-established Models

Analytics Objective 1 intends to A/B test revisions of the current advertising for the Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch within The Collins Concierge, the department’s weekly newsletter. Specifically, it will test if an image-based or video-based ad will increase “Reserve a Table” clicks in comparison to the current text-only format. After extensive research, three established frameworks inform how that test will be built and executed. AO1 will examine the email response process, visual attention and heuristics, and cognitive load and information overload.

Email marketing response occurs in a sequence, wherein a reader first sees a message, engages with it, and then chooses whether to act on it. Hartemo’s newsletter testing model focuses on this response process, linking the factors that affect response to the metrics that measure each step (Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala 2016). This study tests eight format variations against a control group. The format of this analysis easily applies directly to the comparison of image and video templates against RKR’s current section, which employs a controlled format test with a no-graphic baseline.

A review of Kumar’s framework divides newsletter success into relational metrics, such as opens and clicks, and transactional metrics, such as purchases (Kumar 2021). Drawing on 811 newsletters sent to 19,678 loyalty program members, the study determines that design significantly shaped response, and clicks had the strongest relationship to eventual purchase (Kumar 2021). This point supports using click-through rate as AO1’s primary metric, with reservations as the secondary, validating measure. With respect to RKR, Kumar’s sequence would apply to three measurable stages: newsletter views in Canva, “Reserve a Table” clicks, and OpenTable reservations.

One point of note: the response process also exposes a gap AO1 has to account for. Since RKR welcomes walk-ins and accepts Bronco Bucks, some readers will move from acknowledging the new template section and move directly to a visit without ever clicking. Therefore, version-specific links or perhaps a “How did you hear about us?” question at booking help capture that path, but would require additional points in the customer journey to address this variable.

As can be expected, readers do not scan a newsletter evenly or in its entirety. Described in detail by Kumar, visual heuristics guide where the eye lands and subsequently what gets clicked. This study details how newsletter readers follow a U-shaped pattern rather than the Z-pattern typical of web pages. It also outlines how the upper-left region produces higher CTR than links placed elsewhere (Kumar and Salo 2018). In the current RKR section, “view the menu” is a clickable link at the top center while the “Reserve a Table” button sits at the bottom, below the hours. Because placement carries its own documented effect, both test versions keep the button in the same position; otherwise a change in clicks could come from placement rather than media. Using current metrics as a baseline, AO1 will test relocation of the clickable “Reserve a Table” button for the remainder of the fall, and media additions through the sixteen weeks of Spring.

With regard to adding media to the RKR section of The Collins Concierge, Imagery is known to compete strongly for attention once an email is open. Skourou’s study using eye-tracking technique and tools found that large images captured more attention than discount codes and prices in promotional emails. Notably, what readers chose to look at mapped to their purchase decisions (Skourou and Spiliotopoulos 2024). This supports visual content as AO1’s main test variable, since the current section depends on a block of text to communicate its key details, specifically food and its accompanying atmosphere. On the contrary, the study also shows that a strong image or video could consequently draw focus away from the button it is meant to support.

Industry guides from Semrush and OpenTable support the aforementioned notion. High-quality images are most recommended, coupled with contrasting CTAs, and testing one variable at a time over at least two weeks (Go 2024). OpenTable’s restaurant guide adds that key information belongs at the top, supported by strong food photos and bold CTA buttons (Jones 2023). For RKR, Chef Matt’s seasonal dishes offer natural subject matter for either format.

This objective intends to be mindful of the potential for cognitive overload and the possibility to annoy or turn-off the target audience. Visual content can compete for a reader’s limited attention rather than enhance or entice. A large field experiment found that while GIFs and emojis did not affect CTR individually, combining them inadvertently increased unsubscribes, as the elements competed for the same cognitive resources (Bashirzadeh, Mai, and Faure 2022). As such, AO1 aims to add only one visual element at a time. The image and video templates will match in layout, copy, and button placement, making media the only variable.

Research for this objective also flags the potential for inbox overload. Several studies found university recipients reported receiving 30 bulk emails in a single week, often opening them without reading and trashing 22% of newsletters (Kong, Zhu, and Konstan 2021). At one business school, academics received 324 organizational bulk emails in a single year with no option to unsubscribe (Bicudo De Castro 2025). As such, if Collins Concierge readers are facing similar volume in addition to academic workload, this objective must acknowledge that a redesign may not move CTR regardless of format. This is why AO1 measures clicks per view directly rather than relying on open rates.

Email also struggles when it lacks a clear role in the audience’s decision process. Survey respondents reacted with resistance and irritation toward email marketing that did not fit their customer journey (Zunac, Miletic, and Kozina 2022). The results of this study justify treating the redesign as one input toward reservations rather than its sole driver.

Adequateness of Gathered Information

The information above is significantly adequate in addressing the low click-rate of RKR’s newsletter channel. It addresses the potential roadblocks in attracting the attention need to gain awareness, which is overall design and aesthetics, particularly as it relates to the placement of the desired goal, which it button location, but also fatigue since the section does not change and does not employ eye-catching media. On the other hand, it raises red flags with regard to extenuating circumstances which may supercede the design optimization, which are out of RKR’s control such as inbox overload. The studies align with industry suggestions, all of which are actionable and applicable to the business problem. The only biases are really in the industry guides from Semrush and OpenTable, since they are businesses providing free resources to sway readers into purchasing services (Go 2024), (Jones 2023). Additionally, the eye-tracking study had a very small pool of participants, and the Zunac study of the effectiveness of email as a single marketing channel was largely comprised of female participants, making the data somewhat biased (Skourou and Spiliotopoulos 2024), (Zunac, Miletic, and Kozina 2022). This research will be applied to revising the RKR section of The Collins Concierge, by addressing button placement and aesthetics. Beginning with a baseline of the previous issue’s metrics, Fall will test only relocation of the button to the upper left, and Spring will A/B test video versus image.

Need for Additional Analysis

Since the gathered information was largely sufficient but missing data specific to the Concierge’s audience, additional analysis is needed to fully address the AO. None of the reviewed studies looked at a restaurant section inside a university newsletter, so primary data will fill that gap. Beginning with a baseline of CTR from previous Concierge issues pulled from Canva, Fall will measure the effect of moving the “Reserve a Table” button to the upper left of the current text-only section, and Spring will A/B test image versus video, alternating weekly with the button in the same position. Page views will be tracked alongside clicks, since the university studies suggest inbox overload could keep readers from ever reaching the RKR section; this will help determine whether low CTR is a design problem or a readership problem (Kong, Zhu, and Konstan 2021), (Bicudo De Castro 2025). Each version will also use its own link to OpenTable so reservations can be tied back to the format that drove them. On the other hand, clicks will not capture everyone, particularly guests who walk in or pay with Bronco Bucks, so a “How did you hear about us?” question at booking will help account for those visits. Holidays, finals, and campus events will be noted throughout, since alternating weekly means outside factors could affect results. Click rates between versions will be compared using a two-proportion test to confirm whether differences are meaningful.

Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

The original AO set out to A/B test two RKR section formats in The Collins Concierge from October 2026 to June 2027, comparing “Reserve a Table” click rates and attributed OpenTable reservations between versions. It still holds, but the research has narrowed it, particularly as it relates to what is being tested and when. It addresses RKR’s need to build sustainable demand by improving a section that is currently easy to scroll past, with no imagery and a button placed at the bottom, below the hours. On the other hand, testing media and button placement at the same time would make it impossible to know which change caused an increase, so the AO will be split into two phases. Two other approaches were considered. A factorial test would compare every combination of button placement and media at once [@hartemo2016]. However, it would require splitting the mailing list into four groups, leaving too few issues per version within one semester. A bundled redesign would be simpler, but it would not show which change made the difference. As such, the two-phase approach is the most practical option for isolating one change at a time. Beginning with a baseline of CTR from previous issues, Fall will test only the relocation of the button to the upper left, and Spring will A/B test video versus image, alternating weekly with the button in the same position. Canva will be used to track page views and clicks, which is necessary for separating a design problem from a readership problem, and each version will use its own link to OpenTable to tie reservations back to the format. A two-proportion test will compare click rates between versions, since it is a simple and appropriate way to determine whether a difference is real or due to chance. These tools are appropriate because they are already available to RKR and the Concierge team, they require no individual reader data, and they follow the same steps a reader takes from viewing the newsletter to clicking to booking (Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala 2016).

2.1.2 AO2. Customer Experience Factors Associated With Overall Satisfaction (Carmen Jimenez)

Analytics Objective: Using anonymous post-visit survey responses, compare RKR guests’ ratings of food quality, service quality, and atmosphere/physical environment to identify the strongest and weakest experience areas.

Existence of Well-established Models

Customer satisfaction is generally understood as a guest’s overall evaluation of a dining experience. In restaurant settings, this evaluation is usually influenced by several parts of the experience rather than by one factor alone. For AO2, the most relevant dimensions are food quality, service quality, and atmosphere or the physical environment. These dimensions provide a useful framework for understanding what RKR guests value most and where improvements may be needed.

A strong framework for AO2 comes from Ryu, Lee, and Kim, who examined how food quality, service quality, and the physical environment contribute to restaurant image, perceived value, customer satisfaction, and behavioral intentions (Ryu, Lee, and Kim 2012). This framework is especially useful for AO2 because it brings together the three main experience dimensions that RKR plans to measure. Instead of evaluating the dining experience only through food or only through service, the framework treats the restaurant experience as multidimensional. This supports the structure of the RKR survey and allows the team to compare different parts of the guest experience using the same rating scale.

For RKR, this multidimensional approach is important because the restaurant experience includes more than the meal itself. Guests interact with the food, the service staff, and the restaurant environment during the same visit. A guest may rate one of these areas very positively while rating another area less favorably. Looking at the dimensions separately can therefore provide more useful information than relying only on one overall satisfaction question. The framework also supports the use of overall satisfaction as a broader measure that can be considered alongside the individual experience dimensions.

Food quality is one of the most established components of restaurant satisfaction. Namkung and Jang found that food quality is associated with customer satisfaction and behavioral intentions in restaurant settings (Namkung and Jang 2007). Food quality can include characteristics such as taste, freshness, presentation, temperature, portion size, and consistency. These characteristics help explain why food should be evaluated as its own part of the dining experience rather than being combined with service or atmosphere.

This approach is relevant to AO2 because the survey can ask RKR guests to evaluate their perception of the food experience directly. Ratings of food quality can then be compared with ratings of service quality and atmosphere or physical environment. If food receives the highest average ratings, it may represent a current strength of the restaurant. If it receives lower ratings than the other experience areas, the results may identify an opportunity for improvement. However, the food-quality approach alone is too narrow to fully address AO2 because the objective examines the overall dining experience through several dimensions.

Service quality is another important component of restaurant customer satisfaction. Ryu, Lee, and Kim’s framework treats service quality separately from food quality and the physical environment (Ryu, Lee, and Kim 2012). This distinction is useful because a guest can enjoy the food while still having a less positive experience with service, or the opposite. Service quality may involve friendliness, attentiveness, responsiveness, professionalism, communication, and reliability.

Service quality is particularly relevant to RKR because the restaurant operates within The Collins College of Hospitality Management and also functions as a learning environment. Guests are still customers of the restaurant and evaluate the service they receive as part of their dining experience. Measuring service quality separately can help RKR identify whether guests view service as one of the strongest parts of the experience or whether certain aspects may need attention. For AO2, service ratings will therefore be compared with food-quality and atmosphere ratings rather than being interpreted in isolation.

Atmosphere and the physical environment represent another established area of restaurant research. Han and Ryu examined relationships among the physical environment, price perception, customer satisfaction, and restaurant loyalty (Han and Ryu 2009). Heung and Gu also examined the influence of restaurant atmospherics on customer evaluations and behavioral responses (Heung and Gu 2012). Together, these studies support including the physical environment as a separate dimension of the dining experience.

The physical environment may include elements such as cleanliness, décor, lighting, seating, layout, comfort, and the overall atmosphere created by the restaurant. For RKR, this dimension may also reflect the restaurant’s campus setting and the overall feeling guests experience during lunch or dinner service. These elements are different from the food and service themselves, but they can still contribute to how guests evaluate the visit.

The physical-environment approach is useful for AO2 because it allows RKR to identify whether the atmosphere is evaluated as positively as the food and service. However, similar to the food-quality approach, it is not sufficient by itself to answer the full analytics objective. AO2 requires a broader comparison of several experience dimensions. For this reason, the multidimensional restaurant-quality framework provides a stronger overall foundation, while the food-quality and physical-environment approaches provide additional support for individual dimensions.

Previous restaurant research also connects customer satisfaction with future behavioral intentions, including intention to return and willingness to recommend a restaurant (Arora and Singer 2006). These measures are relevant to the RKR project because positive dining experiences may contribute to repeat visits and positive recommendations. However, AO2 will treat intention to return and willingness to recommend as secondary descriptive indicators rather than as evidence of actual future behavior. A guest stating that they intend to return does not confirm that a repeat visit will actually occur.

Perceived value also appears in several restaurant models, including the framework used by Ryu, Lee, and Kim (Ryu, Lee, and Kim 2012). However, perceived value will not be treated as a primary dimension in the current AO2. The revised objective is intentionally focused on food quality, service quality, and atmosphere or physical environment. Keeping these three dimensions as the main areas of comparison makes the objective more focused and directly connected to the planned survey.

Taken together, the existing research provides a strong conceptual foundation for AO2. The multidimensional restaurant-quality framework is the strongest overall fit because it directly includes the three experience dimensions that RKR plans to compare. The food-quality and physical-environment approaches provide additional support for understanding individual parts of the guest experience. These models will guide the design of the anonymous post-visit survey and the interpretation of the results.

The survey will use five-point rating items to measure food quality, service quality, atmosphere and physical environment, overall satisfaction, intention to return, and willingness to recommend. Open-ended questions will also allow guests to identify the best part of their experience and areas that could be improved. The existing research therefore helps determine what should be measured, but it cannot determine which experience areas are actually strongest or weakest at RKR.

This limitation is important because the previous studies were conducted in restaurant settings that differ from RKR. RKR is a student-operated restaurant located on a university campus and serves its own mix of guests. The existing models can guide the research design, but primary survey data from RKR guests are still necessary to understand the restaurant’s specific customer experience. For that reason, the literature provides the framework for AO2, while the RKR survey will provide the evidence needed to identify strengths and improvement opportunities.

Adequateness of Gathered Information

The gathered information is sufficient to identify the main dimensions that should be measured for AO2, including food quality, service quality, atmosphere or physical environment, overall satisfaction, and future behavioral intentions. The reviewed studies are generally consistent in showing that these dimensions are important parts of the restaurant experience, and several of the sources are directly based on restaurant settings (Han and Ryu 2009; Heung and Gu 2012; Namkung and Jang 2007; Ryu, Lee, and Kim 2012). However, the existing research is not sufficient to determine which dimensions RKR guests currently evaluate most positively or which areas need the most improvement. The studies were conducted in different restaurant contexts and populations, so their findings cannot be assumed to apply directly to RKR. Primary survey data from RKR guests are therefore necessary to complete the objective. Possible limitations of the planned survey include convenience sampling, nonresponse bias, and the possibility that guests with a connection to Cal Poly Pomona or RKR may provide more favorable responses. The existing literature will therefore be used to guide what is measured, while the RKR survey will provide the restaurant-specific evidence needed to identify strengths and improvement opportunities.

Need for Additional Analysis

Additional analysis is needed because the existing research cannot determine which parts of the RKR dining experience are currently strongest or weakest for its own guests. To address this gap, anonymous post-visit survey responses will be analyzed using response counts, percentages, and average ratings for food quality, service quality, atmosphere or physical environment, and overall satisfaction. Open-ended comments will also be reviewed and grouped into recurring themes to provide additional context about what guests value and what they believe could be improved. Intention to return and willingness to recommend will be summarized as secondary descriptive indicators. If the number of responses is sufficient, simple exploratory correlations may also be used to describe how the experience dimensions are associated with overall satisfaction. These analyses will not be interpreted as causal evidence. The additional primary-data analysis will allow RKR to apply the existing research framework to its own guests and identify specific customer-experience priorities that cannot be determined from the literature alone.

Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

The current AO2 remains appropriate because it directly addresses RKR’s need to understand which parts of the guest experience are performing well and which areas may require improvement. The objective is measurable using anonymous post-visit survey responses and is closely aligned with PO2, which focuses on identifying what RKR guests value most and where improvements are needed in the overall dining experience.

To accomplish AO2, the analysis will use descriptive statistics to compare guest ratings of food quality, service quality, atmosphere or physical environment, and overall satisfaction. Response counts, percentages, and average ratings will be used to identify the highest- and lowest-rated experience areas. Open-ended comments will also be reviewed and organized into recurring themes to provide context for the numerical results and identify specific strengths or improvement opportunities mentioned by guests.

Intention to return and willingness to recommend will be included as secondary descriptive indicators. If the sample size is sufficient, simple exploratory correlations may also be used to examine whether higher ratings in food quality, service quality, or atmosphere are associated with higher overall satisfaction. These relationships will be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

These analytical techniques are appropriate because they match the type of data expected from the survey and directly support the purpose of AO2. The descriptive analysis will allow RKR to compare major experience dimensions in a clear and actionable way, while the open-ended responses can help explain why guests rated certain areas more positively or negatively. The optional exploratory correlations can provide additional insight into which experience dimensions appear most closely associated with overall satisfaction. Together, these methods will help RKR identify customer-experience priorities and make evidence-based decisions about where improvements may have the greatest value.

2.1.3 AO3.Facebook Content and Messaging Strategies and Reservation Performance (Luis Ahumada)

Analytics Objective: Analyze associations between facebook content and messaging strategies, engagement metrics, and OpenTable reservation activity.

Existence of Well-established Models (2-3 pages per AO)

There are several types of models and theories that can support AO3 and help explain why different Facebook content and messaging may lead to different levels of customer engagement. The key ideas that are connected to A03 are digital consumer engagement, Media Richness, Speech Act Theory, processing fluency, the Theory of Reasoned Action, and customer behavioral response. Together these ideas help explain how customers process social media content, how the way a message is presented can affect engagement, and why engagement does not always lead directly to an actual reservation. These theories are important to AO3 because the objective looks past simply identifying which Facebook posts receive the most engagement and also considers whether those patterns are connected to OpenTable reservation activity. 

Processing fluency helps explain why visual representation of content may affect engagement. Philp, Jacobson, and Pance found that consumers responded better to food images that were easier to recognize and understand (Philp, Jacobson, and Pancer 2022a). Drossos, Coursaris, and Kagiouli’s study found that Facebook posts using images and emotional or transformational appeals had a higher rate of engagement (Drossos, Coursaris, and Kagiouli 2024). Their study also showed that posts with higher interaction did not always perform better. Together, these findings support AO3 because they show that Facebook performance can depend on different visuals and content characteristics, not just the topic of the content or messaging. 

Media Richness Theory and Speech Act Theory help explain why the way a message is communicated can play a factor in a customer’s response. Manningham, Asselin, and Bourguignon performed a study on 639 Facebook posts from different restaurants and analyzed the wording, post format, and use of emojis (Manningham, Asselin, and Bourguignon 2024a).The finding was that direct and expressive wording, along with emoji use, was tied to higher customer engagement. Velosa and Gomez-Suarez also found that when management responses matched the original social media content, customers showed higher engagement and stronger booking intention (Veloso and Gomez-Suarez 2023). These findings support AO3 because they show that customer response can really depend on how content is written and presented, not just the type of content being posted. This means that when analyzing RKR Facebook content, it would make sense to compare both the type of content and the way the message within the content is communicated.

Digital consumer engagement is also important because it shows us that not every type of engagement has the same definition behind it. Halloran and Lutz found that stronger forms of engagement, like customers commenting on a post, were more closely related to restaurant purchase frequency. Weaker measures like likes had less of a relationship with restaurant visit frequency (Halloran and Lutz 2021a).This supports AO3 because it allows us to see that not every Facebook metric can be treated equally when deciding which strategies perform best. Yost, Zhang, and Qi also found that social media engagement was related to sales, but engagement did not explain all of the challenges in business performance (Yost, Zhang, and Qi 2021). These findings show that engagement can be useful for AO3, but it should not be used on its own to determine whether a specific Facebook marketing strategy is successful or not, instead tying it to reservation activity can help support the final decision. 

The Theory of Reasoned Act and customer behavioral response explain why customer intention shouldn’t be treated the same as actual behavior. Hanaysha’s study found that interactivity, relevance, informativeness, and entertainment were positively related to brand engagement, and the higher engagement was tied to higher purchase intention (Hanaysha 2022). So this supports the idea that social media content can affect consumer response, but the challenge is that  the study measured intention instead of actual customer behavior. Simonetti and Bigne also found a similar result when they performed a study measuring restaurant-related social media cues. Their findings showed that restaurant images were important for capturing initial attention, while reviews and ratings also played a factor on how customers evaluated the restaurant (Simonetti and Bigne 2022). These findings challenge AO3 because they tell us that a customer can respond in a positive manner to a content being posted, but this doesn’t necessarily mean that they intend to visit the restaurant without actually making a reservation. Again, this is why looking at more than just Facebook engagement is important for AO3, as it will strengthen the final decision on what Facebook Strategy works best. 

A separate challenge that was brought up was that customer engagement might also be influenced by activity on other social media platforms. Unnava and Aravindakshan studied Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram and found that engagement on one platform could be affected by activity on another platform (Unnava and Aravindakshan 2021). Another finding was that the effects that each platform has on each other isn’t limited to a specific amount of sessions, this effect can continue over time. This is connected to AO3 because it shows us that changes in Facebook engagement or reservation activity may not be connected to Facebook on its own. RKR customers might also be exposed to content on Instagram, Youtube, CPP Newsletters, CPP Website, etc. playing a role on the customers decision of visiting the restaurant or making the reservation. Because of this, Facebook metrics should be interpreted carefully when comparing with OpenTable activity. 

Overall, the research supports the main idea behind AO3, but also shows that Facebook performance should not be judged by engagement alone. The studies show that visual presentation, message style, content characteristics, and different types of engagement can play a role in how consumers respond to social media content. At the same time, the challenging studies show that engagement does not always lead to conversion because there are other factors that play a role in influencing a consumer. These factors can be purchase intention, brand attitude, information quality, and activity on other platforms. As a result of these challenges , AO3 should compare Facebook content and messaging strategies using both engagement metrics and OpenTable reservation activity instead of relying on one type of measure on its own. 

Adequateness of Gathered Information

The information gathered for AO3 is adequate because the sources cover the key ideas that are important to the objective. These key ideas include Facebook content, messaging style, engagement, restaurant behavior, and booking or purchase intent. Some of the studies used are very relevant because they focus directly on Facebook or restaurant settings, like the work of Manningham, Asselin, and Bourguignon and Halloran and Lutz (Manningham, Asselin, and Bourguignon 2024b); (Halloran and Lutz 2021b). The research also used different methods, including content analysis, surveys, experiments, eye tracking, and regression analysis, which provides different types of evidence that can support AO3. There were also some studies that did not hold the same level of quality because the studies performed focused on hotels, Instagram, or other social media platforms instead of Facebook to restaurant activity. They also differed on what was being measured, such as purchase intention, visit intention, or booking intention rather than actual customer behavior. Overall, the research is strong enough to support AO3, but it does not fully answer whether Facebook engagement is connected to actual OpenTable activity, which shows why there is additional analysis that is needed. 

Need for Additional Analysis

Additional analysis is still needed because the research gathered does not completely show how Facebook affects customer response at RKR. The studies show that social media content and messaging can affect engagement, attention, and purchase or booking intent, but many of them don’t measure actual reservations or visits. For my part of the project, I will focus on RKR’s Facebook data by comparing different content types, messaging styles, and engagement metrics with available OpenTable Activity. Trackable links or QR codes can also help show if Facebook activity is connected to reservation behavior at RKR. Overall, this analysis will show what role Facebook may have within RKR’s larger digital marketing strategy.

Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

Based on the reviewed research, AO3 should remain the same because it directly supports RKR’s larger goal of building sustainable demand. AO3 focuses on Facebook and whether specific content and messaging strategies are connected to stronger engagement and OpenTable reservation activity. 

To complete AO3, I plan to organize RKR’s Facebook posts into different content and messaging categories and compare how they perform using metrics such as likes, comments, shares, link clicks. I can then compare these results with available OpenTable activity to see if specific Facebook Strategies are also connected to stronger reservation related behavior. These methods allow me to look at both Facebook engagement and customer behavior instead of only using social media metrics. This approach also fits with the larger project because it uses both social media performance and reservation data. 

2.1.4 AO4. Website Content, Navigation, and Usability (Georgia Monjarrez)

Existence of Well-established Models

Website usability is relevant to RKR because prospective guests need practical information before deciding whether and when to visit. This objective examines three specific activities: finding the menu, identifying operating hours, and reaching the reservation process. The literature provides complementary perspectives on technology acceptance, information quality, and usability measurement. Together, these perspectives explain why the study should assess both what visitors can accomplish and how they evaluate the experience. The following applications to RKR are proposed research choices rather than findings about its current website.

Perceived ease of use and usefulness. Davis’s technology acceptance research distinguishes perceived usefulness from perceived ease of use and develops measures of both constructs. The study reports relationships between these perceptions and system use, with usefulness showing a stronger relationship than ease of use (Davis 1989). This distinction matters because a website can feel simple to navigate while failing to provide information that helps a visitor make a decision. Conversely, useful information may require substantial effort to find. The original research concerns information technology acceptance rather than restaurant reservations, so it provides a theoretical starting point rather than direct evidence about RKR guests.

For this project, perceived ease will be assessed immediately after each task by asking how easy or difficult it was to complete. A separate overall item will ask whether the website provided the information needed to plan a visit. These questions address different judgments: effort and usefulness. For example, locating a menu quickly does not establish whether its contents meet a visitor’s information needs. The proposed brief items adapt the concepts to RKR; they will not be described as the complete validated Davis scales. Pilot feedback should establish whether participants understand the wording and response options.

Information quality and hospitality decisions. Jeong and Lambert evaluated an information-quality framework using eight hypothetical lodging websites and 240 conference attendees. Their findings identified perceived usefulness and attitudes as significant indicators of customers’ purchase-related behavior within that study (Jeong and Lambert 2001). This hospitality application supports examining information as part of a visitor’s decision process, rather than treating a website only as a promotional display. However, simulated hotel websites and conference attendees differ from a student-operated restaurant and its prospective guests. The study therefore motivates local investigation without establishing that the same relationships or effect sizes apply to RKR.

For RKR, the proposed assessment will distinguish finding a page from finding the correct information. A menu task will require participants to identify the relevant menu, and an hours task will require them to state the posted hours for a specified service period. Before testing, the research team will verify the correct answers against the current website and record the testing date. This procedure should help distinguish a navigation problem from unclear or inconsistent content. Participant comments can identify information they expected but could not find; the team should verify those observations before recommending a content change.

Information systems success. DeLone and McLean’s updated information systems success model provides a broader framework for evaluating systems and discusses its application to electronic commerce (DeLone and McLean 2003). Its relevance here is that website success requires an explicit definition of the outcomes being evaluated. AO4 will focus on a limited part of the customer journey: successful access to dining information and the reservation interface. It will not claim to test the entire information systems success model.

This boundary is important for interpreting the proposed results. A participant who reaches the reservation interface has completed the navigation task, even if no suitable table is available. A participant who reports that the website is helpful has expressed a perception, not made a booking. Reservation completion, revenue, and repeat patronage require additional evidence beyond this usability exercise. Consequently, the project objective is to recommend improvements that support access; any later claim that those improvements increase reservations would require implementation and follow-up measurement.

Usability as performance and perception. Hornbæk’s review of 180 usability studies emphasizes the need to distinguish and compare objective performance measures with subjective evaluations. It also highlights problems with treating usability too narrowly or using measures without sufficient justification (Hornbæk 2006). This supports collecting several complementary measures for AO4: task success, elapsed time, and perceived ease. These measures should be reported separately because a visitor can succeed slowly, fail quickly, or complete a task while finding the process frustrating.

The proposed study will calculate unassisted completion as the number of participants who finish a task correctly without help divided by the number who attempt it. Median completion time in seconds will summarize successful, unassisted attempts; assisted attempts, unsuccessful attempts, and timeouts will be reported separately. Immediately after every attempted task, participants will rate ease from 1 (very difficult) to 5 (very easy). Navigation observations and a short open-ended question will help explain the quantitative results. These operational definitions make the objective measurable while preserving the distinction between observed behavior and self-reported experience.

Adequateness of Gathered Information

The selected scholarly sources provide a foundation for choosing constructs and measures, but they cannot establish how well the current RKR website serves its users. They include foundational information-systems research, a usability review, and hospitality website research; their age and differing contexts limit direct transfer to contemporary mobile browsing and RKR’s audience. Existing evidence is therefore adequate for developing the study but insufficient for answering AO4. Primary observations and post-task survey responses are needed from prospective guests, including campus and community participants where feasible. Prior familiarity with RKR and the website should be recorded because experienced users may navigate differently from first-time visitors.

Need for Additional Analysis

Participants will attempt the three tasks from the same starting page, using neutral instructions that do not reveal where to click. The team will pilot the procedure, set a consistent time limit before main data collection, vary task order across participants, and record device type and prior website familiarity. Timing will stop at success, a request for help, abandonment, or the time limit. The reservation task will end when the participant reaches the interface for beginning a reservation; no purchase or booking is required. For each task, analysis will report the success numerator and denominator, completion percentage, median successful completion time, and distribution of ease ratings, alongside recurring navigation problems. A proposed benchmark of 80% unassisted completion will be applied separately to each task; this is a project planning target, not a threshold established by the cited studies. Missing responses and technical failures will be documented separately from navigation failures.

Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

AO4 remains appropriate because it connects PO4 to three observable tasks and defined measures. The reviewed frameworks support distinguishing useful information, perceived ease, and observed performance. They do not establish which changes RKR needs; primary testing will supply that evidence. Two descriptive research questions guide the assessment: How successfully can prospective guests locate the menu, identify operating hours, and reach the reservation interface, and does each task meet the proposed 80% unassisted completion target? Which content or navigation difficulties accompany unsuccessful attempts, longer successful completion times, or lower ease ratings?

Recommendations will link each observed problem to a specific proposed change and a corresponding measure for follow-up testing. For example, difficulty locating hours may justify clearer placement or labeling, while trouble reaching the reservation widget may justify a more visible entry point. These are possible recommendations to evaluate rather than conclusions about the current website. A later test using the same task definitions would be needed to assess improvement after implementation.

The objective is primarily descriptive, so this review does not require separate causal hypotheses. Results from a convenience sample will describe the tested participants, with device type and prior familiarity considered during interpretation. The three tasks completed by one participant will not be treated as three independent participants. Successful navigation, perceived usefulness, completed reservations, and revenue remain distinct outcomes. This scope allows AO4 to support the group’s reservation goal while keeping its conclusions proportional to the data collected.

2.1.5 AO5. Instagram Content and Engagement Analysis (Spencer Conway)

Analytics Objective: This analytics objective will determine which Instagram content format produces the highest engagement rate for Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch. First, past posts will be grouped by format to establish a performance baseline. RKR will then test new content in selected formats and compare its performance with the baseline. Engagement rate will be calculated consistently using likes, comments, shares, and saves divided by reach, where Instagram Insights data are available. The findings will guide recommendations about which formats RKR should prioritize in future Instagram posts.

Existence of Well-established Models

There are a few theories and research approaches that can help support AO5. The main ideas that connect to this objective are customer engagement, the Stimulus-Organism-Response model, inspiration, and visual presentation on social media. These ideas help explain why different Instagram posts or formats may get different reactions from customers.

Lee and Kwak (2026) studied restaurant social media and found that the way food is shown can affect customer inspiration and engagement.(Lee and Kwak 2026) Outcome-focused food images performed better than process-focused images in their study. This is useful for AO5 because it shows that the way restaurant content is presented can make a difference in how people respond to it.

Bushara et al. (2023) used the Stimulus-Organism-Response model to study restaurant social media. (Bushara et al. 2023)Their study found that things like entertainment, interaction, customization, and trendiness can affect perceived value and customer behavior. This connects to AO5 because RKR’s Instagram posts can be viewed as the stimulus and likes, comments, shares, and saves can be viewed as customer responses. One limitation is that Instagram Insights does not tell us exactly what a customer was thinking or feeling before engaging with a post.

Philp, Jacobson, and Pancer (2022) also looked directly at restaurant food marketing on Instagram.(Philp, Jacobson, and Pancer 2022b) They found that the visual characteristics of food images were connected to likes and comments. This supports AO5 because it shows that actual Instagram post data can be used to compare different types of content and see which characteristics are connected to stronger engagement.

Kulikovskaja et al. (2023) found that different types of social media content can lead to different types of customer engagement. (Kulikovskaja et al. 2023) This is important because RKR should not treat every Instagram post the same way. A Reel, carousel, or single-image post may give customers a different experience and may also create different levels of engagement.

Chan, Chen, and Leung (2023) also found that visual presentation can affect how customers respond to restaurant social media.(chan2023?) Their research showed that factors such as visual variety and movement can make a difference. This relates to AO5 because Instagram formats have different visual characteristics. For example, a Reel uses movement and video, while a regular post is more static.

Overall, the research supports the idea that the way restaurant social media content is presented can affect customer engagement. However, the existing research does not tell us exactly which Instagram format will work best for RKR. This is why analyzing RKR’s own Instagram data is still needed.

Adequateness of Gathered Information

The information gathered so far is enough to support the direction of AO5. The research shows that restaurant social media content, visual presentation, and content type can affect engagement. Some of the studies also focus directly on Instagram or restaurant social media, which makes them useful for this project. However, the research cannot tell us which format works best specifically for RKR. Different restaurants have different audiences and different types of content, so RKR’s own Instagram data still needs to be analyzed.

Need for Additional Analysis

Additional analysis is needed to compare RKR’s actual Instagram performance. I plan to group past posts into formats such as single-image posts, carousels, and Reels or videos. I will then collect available engagement metrics such as likes, comments, shares, saves, and reach. Engagement rate will be calculated using the same method across posts so the formats can be compared more fairly.

After creating a baseline from past posts, RKR can also test new content in selected formats and compare the results with the historical performance. This should help show whether certain Instagram formats consistently perform better for RKR.

Assessment and Affirmation of Analytics Objectives

Based on the research, AO5 should remain the same. The research supports the idea that different social media formats and visual characteristics can affect customer engagement, but there is still a need to test this using RKR’s own Instagram data.

To complete AO5, I plan to compare RKR’s Instagram formats using engagement rate. Posts will be grouped by format and compared using likes, comments, shares, saves, and reach where the data is available. The research models will help explain why some formats may perform differently, while the actual Instagram data will be used to determine which formats work best for RKR.

The final goal is to give RKR a more data-driven Instagram strategy and recommend which formats they should prioritize moving forward. The results will focus on Instagram engagement and will not assume that higher engagement automatically means more restaurant reservations or sales.

3 Progress Report 3 - CHAPTER 2: BACKGROUND AND ANALYTICS OBJECTIVES

3.1 Client (Company) Background

The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch (RKR) is located at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona, and is part of The Collins College of Hospitality Management. Established in 1990, RKR has traditionally operated as a student-managed restaurant and learning laboratory where hospitality students gain hands-on experience in restaurant operations, food preparation, customer service, and management (California State Polytechnic University, Pomona n.d.).

RKR is transitioning toward a dual operating model that combines its educational purpose with stand-alone restaurant operations. According to the initial project proposal prepared by Dr. Linchi Kwok, this emerging model may allow the restaurant to operate with paid staff on three weekdays while continuing to serve as a classroom laboratory on designated instructional days(Kwok 2026).

This transition represents an important business challenge because stand-alone restaurant services must generate sufficient customer demand and revenue to support financially sustainable operations. Therefore, attracting guests, increasing reservation activity, and encouraging repeat visits are important priorities while maintaining RKR’s educational identity (Kwok 2026).

3.1.1 Company Mission/Vision

RKR’s educational mission is closely connected to Cal Poly Pomona’s emphasis on experiential learning. The restaurant provides students with opportunities to apply classroom knowledge in a professional dining environment, develop practical hospitality skills, and gain experience serving real customers. Through this learning model, students develop skills in teamwork, leadership, service, and restaurant management (California State Polytechnic University, Pomona n.d.).

Although a separate official mission and vision statement for RKR has not been identified in the available materials, its current strategic direction is outlined in the initial project proposal. RKR seeks to preserve its educational purpose while developing sustainable restaurant operations that can attract customers and generate revenue independently of instructional support (Kwok 2026).

From this perspective, RKR’s long-term direction involves balancing hospitality education with successful restaurant operations. This means continuing to provide meaningful learning opportunities for students while maintaining a dining experience that meets customer expectations and encourages guests to return.

3.1.2 Core Competencies

One of RKR’s main competencies is its ability to combine hospitality education with actual restaurant operations. As part of The Collins College of Hospitality Management, students gain practical experience in different areas of the restaurant, including food preparation, guest service, leadership, and management. This educational connection gives RKR an identity that differs from traditional restaurants(California State Polytechnic University, Pomona n.d.).

Another important strength is the restaurant’s culinary offering and physical environment. RKR features seasonal menus with farm-to-table-inspired dishes, including ingredients sourced from Cal Poly Pomona’s agricultural resources. Its location also provides scenic campus views, creating an attractive atmosphere for guests (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.a).

According to the initial project proposal, RKR also benefits from campus and alumni connections, established social media accounts, and access to reservation information. These resources provide opportunities to reach potential customers, better understand guest behavior, and improve marketing effectiveness.

Additionally, the arrival of a new general manager and executive chef provides an opportunity to strengthen the restaurant’s operations, culinary offerings, and market positioning. However, these strengths alone do not guarantee sufficient customer demand. RKR still needs to better understand its target audiences, customer motivations, and the marketing channels that are most effective in attracting reservations (Kwok 2026).

3.1.3 Value Propositions

RKR offers a distinctive value proposition by combining a restaurant dining experience with the educational identity of Cal Poly Pomona. Guests can enjoy seasonal meals, fresh ingredients, and an attractive campus setting while supporting the professional development of future hospitality leaders (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.b).

Its culinary offerings, restaurant atmosphere, and connection to the university are important elements that may help differentiate RKR from traditional restaurants. These characteristics may appeal to campus audiences, alumni, local residents, and customers looking for a unique dining experience.

However, the initial project proposal identifies an important area that requires further investigation: whether customers are more attracted by RKR’s culinary experience, its educational mission, or a combination of both. Understanding which aspects customers value most can help the restaurant communicate its strengths more effectively and develop marketing messages that appeal to different audiences(Kwok 2026).

Customer perceptions are especially important because the restaurant’s educational identity alone may not be enough to encourage repeat visits. Food quality, service quality, and the physical environment can also influence customer satisfaction and future behavioral intentions. Understanding these elements can help RKR improve the dining experience and strengthen its overall value proposition (Ryu, Lee, and Kim 2012).

3.1.4 Business Objectives

RKR’s main business objective is to develop sustainable customer demand and generate sufficient revenue to support its stand-alone restaurant operations while preserving its educational mission. As the restaurant transitions toward a dual operating model, attracting guests, increasing reservations, and encouraging repeat visits are important priorities (Kwok 2026).

The initial project proposal identifies several objectives that support this direction, including understanding RKR’s market position, identifying priority customer segments, analyzing reservation patterns, evaluating the digital customer journey, and improving marketing effectiveness (Kwok 2026).

Another important priority is understanding and improving the customer experience. Evaluating guest perceptions of food quality, service quality, atmosphere, and overall satisfaction can help RKR identify strengths and opportunities for improvement. Feedback regarding intention to return and willingness to recommend can also provide useful information about customers’ future behavioral intentions (Ryu, Lee, and Kim 2012).

Digital marketing is another key focus. RKR needs to better understand how its website, email communications, and social media content contribute to customer engagement and reservation-related activity. Analyzing this information can help identify more effective communication strategies and opportunities to improve the customer journey from initial awareness to reservation.

These business priorities provide the foundation for the team’s Capstone Experience Project, which examines newsletter design and reservation activity, customer satisfaction and dining experience, Facebook content performance, website usability, and Instagram engagement.

Together, these areas of investigation support RKR’s broader goal of developing a measurable and repeatable demand-generation system. By using customer feedback, reservation information, and digital marketing performance data, RKR can make more informed decisions about its marketing activities and guest experience while continuing to support hospitality education.

3.2 Description of the Client’s Current Marketing Program

3.2.1 Marketing Team and Expertise

The RKR’s current marketing team is made of several people and platforms rather than being run through one main restaurant marketing team. Current marketing communication includes RKR’s instagram account, The Collins Concierge Newsletter, social channels that are ran by the Collins College of Hospitality marketing team, the RKR website, and third-party platforms such as Google, Yelp, and OpenTable.

Our CEP proposal also identifies that the executive chef is important to RKR’s changing market position, guest experience, and content strategy (Kwok 2026). RKR’s Head Chef has access to his own personal professional Instagram and LinkedIn accounts, which can provide our group another path to highlight the restaurant. Student involvement, and behind the scenes content. The one issue is that the Head Chef does not provide access to his accounts, so they are not identified as official RKR marketing channels. RKR currently has different methods of reaching customers, but as stated before, communication is handled across different people and platforms. So having better coordination between these channels could help RKR maintain a consistent messaging strategy as the restaurant continues to grow.  

3.2.2 Current Target Market

The RKR’s current position and location present a strong opportunity to reach different groups of customers. The connection to the Collins College of Hospitality Management and its Location on Cal Poly Pomona’s campus can present different content strategies that can be used across the different channels that are available. Some groups that could be targeted include students, CPP staff, Pomona corporate companies that could visit the restaurant during official business meetings, and the Pomona community. 

The restaurant can also attract customers who want something that is different from the typical dining experience. Campus-grown ingredients, student managed service, and connections to Cal Poly Pomona’s educational mission gives customers more reasons to visit beyond the food itself. RKR’s seasonal menu and location should also be used to bring in customers who are interested in supporting the university while also going through a fine dining experience. So, although the RKR has the potential to attract a variety of customers, its primary audience has not yet been clearly established by our group. A closer look at reservation activity and digital engagement may provide us with insight into who is interacting with the restaurant and help guide future marketing decisions.

3.2.3 Current Positioning and Perceptual Map

The RKR provides a dining experience that combines fine dining services with the educational mission of Cal Poly Pomona’s Collins College of Hospitality Management. Because RKR is a student operated restaurant, RKR allows students to gain hands-on experience in all aspects of fine dining restaurant operation including making positive guest experiences and services a priority. Its seasonal menu, use of campus grown ingredients, and connection to CPP’s agricultural programs also play a role in what makes the restaurant different from the other fine dining experiences in the surrounding Pomona area. 

RKR’s connection to CPP is a vital part to its identity, but its fine dining experience is just as important when considering the restaurant’s current position in the local market. The RKR offers its guests the opportunity to enjoy a high-quality , carefully prepared meal; while also supporting the professional experience of future hospitality professionals. Together, these elements give the RKR a very unique identity that combines the quality that comes with fine dining and an experience that is tightly connected to the university’s mission. 

In order to examine how the RKR compares with local restaurants, our team developed a perceptual map that includes local surrounding restaurants that fall under teh “fine-dining” category. These restaurants include Pomona Valley Mining Company, Coco Palm, The Derby, and VITA Italian Bar & Grill. The map compares the restaurants based on two dimensions. One being the type of dining experience and the second being the dining atmosphere. The dining experience ranges from traditional to unique, while the dining atmosphere ranges from casual to special occasion or upscale. 

The reason for the RKR’s current placement on the map is because its student-operated setting and connection to CPP helps separate it from its competitors that offer more traditional upscale dining experiences. But, the map also reflects the team’s assessment of each restaurant based on its characteristics rather than customer feedback. Performing more research could help our group determine how guests actually perceive RKR and whether its current positioning on our map aligns with those perceptions of the public. 

3.2.4 Current Product/Services

The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch (RKR) provides public lunch and dinner service within a student-operated hospitality training restaurant at Cal Poly Pomona. Its offering combines seasonal dining, student-delivered service, and views of the campus. The website also promotes the restaurant as a setting for business dinners, family celebrations, and large parties or events. (“The restaurant at kellogg ranch” n.d.).

The published menus include starters, salads, sandwiches, entrées, desserts, and beverages, with dietary options identified. (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.b). Campus partnerships supply ingredients and beverages, including produce from university farms, campus-produced honey, Horsehill wines, and Innovation Brew Works beer. These partnerships help distinguish RKR’s offering through its connection to Cal Poly Pomona and locally sourced food. (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.a).

These characteristics directly support AO2, which compares guest ratings of food quality, service quality, and atmosphere or physical environment. Together, these dimensions represent the core experience RKR provides. The restaurant’s promotional descriptions establish what it offers and emphasizes, while the planned post-visit survey will assess how guests actually evaluate that experience. Seasonal dishes and campus sourcing also provide potential content subjects for the newsletter, Facebook, and Instagram work in AO1, AO3, and AO5.

3.2.5 Current Pricing

RKR’s published fall menus use individual item pricing. Lunch entrées range from $15 to $23, while lunch sandwiches range from $18 to $20. Individual dinner entrées range from $16 to $24, and a sirloin entrée intended for two guests is listed at $48. Desserts are priced at $12 each. These amounts describe listed items rather than complete meal totals. (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.b).

Pricing provides practical information prospective guests can use when planning a visit. This relates to AO4 because finding the menu should give visitors access to relevant dining information, including prices. However, successful navigation does not establish that customers consider those prices affordable or worthwhile. Price perceptions are also outside AO2’s primary comparison of food, service, and atmosphere. The team should therefore describe current prices without claiming that the project will determine an optimal pricing strategy. Pricing rationale, discounts, and private-event rates require client confirmation.

3.2.6 Current Marketing Channels

RKR delivers its dining service directly through its campus restaurant in Building 79 at 3801 West Temple Avenue in Pomona. Its contact page provides location directions, telephone and email contact information, and complimentary parking in Lot L with a reservation. Posted hours are Monday through Friday, 11 a.m.–2 p.m., for lunch and Tuesday through Friday, 5–8 p.m., for dinner, beginning August 24. (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.c).

The website provides an OpenTable reservation widget, while walk-ins are also welcome. (“The restaurant at kellogg ranch” n.d.). The team’s existing report identifies additional customer outreach through The Collins Concierge newsletter, Facebook, and Instagram. These communication channels can introduce guests to RKR and direct them toward dining information or the reservation process.

This channel structure explains the relationship among the project’s AOs. AO1 examines newsletter clicks and attributed reservations; AO3 examines Facebook engagement and its association with OpenTable activity; AO5 compares Instagram engagement across formats. AO4 examines whether visitors can find the menu, identify hours, and reach the reservation interface. These are distinct stages of the customer journey. Reaching the reservation interface does not confirm a booking, and reservation records alone do not capture walk-in visits.

3.2.7 Current Integrated Marketing Communications

RKR’s website emphasizes seasonal food, campus sourcing, hospitality education, welcoming service, and scenic views. It includes guest testimonials and directs visitors to RKR’s Instagram account for team updates, seasonal menu changes, and special events. (“The restaurant at kellogg ranch” n.d.). The sourcing page reinforces the campus connection, while the “Our Story” page presents the restaurant’s educational origins and lists awards and recognitions. (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.a; n.d.d).

The team’s report also documents an RKR promotional section in The Collins Concierge containing menu information, hours, and a reservation link. It identifies Facebook and Instagram as additional channels under investigation. Together, these activities provide several opportunities to communicate the restaurant’s offering and encourage a visit. However, their presence does not establish that messaging, schedules, or reservation links are coordinated across channels.

AO1, AO3, and AO5 address different aspects of communication performance: newsletter design, Facebook content and messaging, and Instagram formats. AO4 complements this work by assessing access to the information and reservation interface that prospective guests need next. The shared implication is that communication should be evaluated through both audience response and subsequent actions where measurable. Higher engagement alone should not be presented as evidence of increased reservations. Client information about campaign planning, content approval, and tracking is needed to assess the integration of RKR’s communications.
